summary:
We developed the Symphony of the Sphere, an interactive web application that bridges the gap between Earth science and auditory art by translating NASA EIC visual frames into real-time, dynamic sonifications. 

The application directly addresses the challenge by offering an intuitive jukebox interface where users can select planetary visualizations such as shifting global temperatures or ocean currents and experience them through a melodius soundscape.

This is crucial because we want to help encourage blind and low-vision communities to engage meaningfully with climate science while uncovering subtle data patterns that visual inspection alone might miss. By fusing software engineering with sound design, we foster a profound emotional connection to our changing planet.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Symphony of the Sphere is an interactive, accessible web application that translates NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into real-time, dynamic audio. The application features an intuitive "jukebox" interface. When a user selects a dataset, a visual playhead line sweeps across the data map. As the line moves, the application reads the pixel data in real-time: warm colors (reds/oranges) are mapped to higher musical pitches, cool colors (blues) map to lower pitches, and dark areas produce silence. The result is a melodious, real-time soundscape that represents the visual data.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact?
The primary benefit is accessibility. Over 2.2 billion people globally live with vision impairment. NASA's climate data is stunning but exclusively visual, leaving this community out of critical climate conversations. Symphony of the Sphere bridges this gap, allowing blind and low-vision users to "hear" the changing climate. Furthermore, it creates a profound emotional connection to the planet for all users. Beyond accessibility, sonification helps uncover subtle data patterns (like sudden temperature spikes) that human eyes might miss when staring at a static heatmap.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML5 for the structural layout, CSS3 for the responsive, high-contrast dark-mode UI design, and TypeScript for the core logic, ensuring type safety and robust performance.
  • Core Audio: The Web Audio API (used to generate live oscillators, manage frequencies, and create the "musical" soundscapes without needing external audio files).
  • Visuals: HTML5 Canvas API (used to draw the visual maps, process the pixel data, and animate the white playhead line).
  • Accessibility: Web Speech API (built-in browser text-to-speech for the screen-reader live log).
  • Live Data: Open-Meteo API and OpenStreetMap Nominatim API (to fetch live, real-time weather data).
  • Tools: Visual Studio Code for development, and Figma Pages for hosting.

How is your project creative?
We didn't just build a standard data dashboard; we built a "Jukebox." We creatively fused software engineering with sound design. Instead of mapping data to random noise, we mapped the visual data to a Pentatonic scale (a 5-note musical scale). This artistic ruleset ensures that even random pixel combinations sound harmonious and musical, rather than chaotic.

What factors did your team consider?
We considered three major factors:

1. Accessibility First: We ensured the entire app is keyboard-navigable (Spacebar to play/stop, numbers to switch datasets), includes a high-contrast mode so blind users know exactly what is on the screen.

2. Performance & Offline Capability: By utilizing TypeScript and the native Canvas API instead of heavy external machine learning libraries, we ensured the website loads instantly and runs smoothly on low-end devices.

3. The Balance of Data and Art: We had to ensure the audio was scientifically accurate (reflecting the actual colors of the map) while remaining pleasant to listen to.
